Yeah, in reality it's a mixture I think. What I think gives the idea precedence is that Trump had less power and spent less money on his campaign, yet through his words, he was able to obtain more power. Now obviously it wasn't only his words, he also had to do a bunch of work, but it seems like somebody with the right words has the power to influence others' minds more than through actions without words. By all means, I may be influenced by a violent person, but then only I'm influenced. But when a few people are influenced by violence and then speak about it and it gets repeated over and over, much like happens here on Voat, that can influence countless people without the masses having had to have experienced those things personally.

Words are just a vehicle. Words like "racist" used to have something powerful backing them up. The word was reinforced by the gravity of the subject matter typically attached to it. People who don't understand this thought they could just use the word, and get the same effect. It did work for a while, back when the word was still largely associated with serious matters. There was a momentum. But now it's associated with "insensitive halloween costumes" and questioning immigration policy. They thought it was the word that was powerful, but it was the subject matter behind the word that was powerful. If you transfer the word to bullshit subject matter, the word becomes bullshit. The people who think "words have power" are the same caliber of people who go to marches and chant slogans, as if yelling "FUCK TRUMP" a thousand times is supposed to change the election results. They're surface-level people doing surface-level activities. Very poor memetics.

Here's something interesting though: now that "racist" and "sexist" and any number of other "ists" have come to be associated with whiny bullshit, there seems to be a void left behind. The things that "racist" used to mean no longer have a word to describe them. If I hear someone say "X is racist", my first thought is "this is going to be some frivolous first-world problem nonsense". There is currently no word that imparts upon me the same thing that "racist" used to. Maybe this is a good thing, at least for a little while. There are no words left to be hijacked. They used them all up. They drained them dry of any and all serious meaning. If there are serious matters to be discussed, they can be discussed a bit more clearly now that there is no potential potential for sensationalizing with spicy words.

And another thought: maybe "racist" (and other ists) being phased out at the moment is reflective of a lack of need for them. When the thing being described by the word becomes less and less common, the word itself is bound to lose relevance. Perhaps these words are simply becoming archaic before our very eyes.

In line with what I understand from your comment - I'm thinking there might be unintended irony with the words Notch chose for his statement. Specifically choice of the word 'narrative'. That word is often used nowadays to negatively characterize a certain idea and is often synonymous with 'propaganda'. Far removed from its actual definition. If that word is overused however just as "racism" and "sexism" are, the meaning or weight of that word too can slide back into irrelevance or meaninglessness from the audience perspective.
